title: Ahalya, seen at last
hookLine: she isn't stone in Valmiki, and two princes bow at her feet
carry: touching feet: honoring the sacred in someone

cards: On television, in comic books, from a grandmother's lap, the scene usually goes like this. A stone lies by the path. Rama's foot brushes it, and the stone becomes a woman.
It's a beautiful picture, and an old one. But it isn't Valmiki's. In Valmiki's Sanskrit there's no stone at all, and no foot brushing against one.
What happens instead is quieter, in some ways more striking, and it starts with a woman nobody can see.

teach.b: Rama walks into the hermitage, with Vishvamitra and Lakshmana behind him, and there she is.

Ahalya, shining with the power of her long penance, the text says, but hidden: like a flame wrapped in smoke, like the moon behind a cloud. Until now, no one could see her at all. Now Rama sees her, and the curse is over.
Then the brothers take hold of Ahalya's feet, the respect you'd show an elder.
Two princes, one of them the prince Hindus worship as Vishnu come to earth, bow at the feet of a woman the world has looked away from for years.
She remembers Gautama's words and receives them as guests, with water for their feet and honor. Flowers fall from the sky. Gautama returns, and they're together again.

Now the version most people grew up with, from later tellings like Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas: Ahalya as a stone, freed by the touch of Rama's foot. Two tellings, and both turn on feet. That's no accident in Hinduism.
Touching the feet, charan sparsh, is how Hindus honor a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a saint, or God's image, and ask for a blessing. Devotees long for the dust of the Lord's feet.
Many teachers read the gesture as bowing to the sacred in that person.

teach.h: IN TULSIDAS: STONE, AND RAMA'S FOOT.
teach.b: In Tulsidas, grace flows from Rama's foot to the stone. In Valmiki it flows the other way too: the prince people worship bows first, at her feet.

teach.h: CHARAN SPARSH: HONOR, AND A BLESSING.

teach.b: That's why, before an exam, a trip or a wedding, you'll see Hindu kids bend to a grandparent's feet, and a hand come down on their heads in blessing.

how: In much of popular Hindu tradition, Ahalya is freed from stone by the touch of Rama's foot, a scene loved for what it says about Rama's grace; Valmiki's version, where she is invisible and freed by hosting him, is often taught alongside it.

s: in Valmiki's Ramayana, Ahalya is turned to stone
she is invisible and doing penance; the stone comes in later tellings.
the honor Hindus give an elder, given here to her.
touching an elder's feet is worship of that person as a god
it honors them and asks a blessing; many teachers read it as bowing to the sacred in them.

games.q: at a family gathering, everyone bends to touch nani's feet. sam whispers: is that worship? by today's story, what fits?
o: it's honor, and asking her blessing; even Rama bowed at Ahalya's feet.
yes, hindus worship their grandparents as gods.
it's an old habit; nobody means anything by it.
games.why: charan sparsh honors the sacred in someone and asks a blessing. in Valmiki, the prince Hindus worship bows at Ahalya's feet.

practice: If you pray, bow, for real or in your mind, at the feet of an image of God or of someone who raised you, and ask a blessing.
If you don't, picture someone you look up to, and someone the world overlooks, and offer each of them the same small bow. Let the honor go both ways.

wordCard.voice: Ahalya restored. Seen at last by Rama, honored at her feet by the princes, and freed as she welcomes them as guests.

orig.note: Sanskrit caraṇa: foot. charan sparsh, touching the feet, honors an elder or the divine and asks a blessing.

carryVoice: Your line: touching feet, honoring the sacred in someone. In Valmiki, Rama bowed first. Day five hundred six, done.
